mainTopic: When a שכיר may swear and collect his wages, and the מגו of רב and שמואל that limits this oath to a hiring done in front of עדים.
overview: חכמים let a שכיר swear and collect his wages because the בעל הבית is busy with many workers and may forget whether he paid. The גמרא tests this reason against two ברייתות. An employer surely remembers the wage he agreed to. After the deadline, he has two חזקות on his side: he does not violate בל תלין, and a worker does not wait to ask for his pay. Next, רב and שמואל (and also רבי יוחנן) limit the worker's oath to cases where the hiring was seen by עדים. Without עדים, the employer is believed through a מגו, since he could have denied hiring him at all. רבא challenges this, saying that by the same logic the Torah's שבועת שומרין would never apply. The answer is that it applies when the deposit was made with a שטר. From this exchange the גמרא learns how a deposit must be returned. Finally, רב ששת finds a ברייתא that seems to contradict רב and שמואל, and רב נחמן בר יצחק begins to answer. His answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Then the worker should also swear about the agreed wage
steps.stepSummary: If the employer is too busy to remember, he could also forget the agreed wage. Yet a ברייתא says the worker must bring proof in a dispute over the agreed amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the worker should also swear when they argue about the agreed wage! Why does a ברייתא teach: a craftsman says 'You agreed to pay me two,' and the employer says 'I agreed to pay only one.' The one who wants to take money from the other must bring proof?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reason it just gave (that the employer is busy and forgets). If that reason is true, it should also apply to a dispute over how much was agreed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason 'בעל הבית טרוד בפועליו' seems to make the employer's memory unreliable in general. But the ברייתא treats a dispute over the agreed amount like a normal monetary claim. There, המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה, and the worker cannot swear and collect. So why doesn't the 'busy employer' reason help the worker here too?

keyTerms.meaning: Whoever wants to take money from another must bring proof
Why then was it taught (in a ברייתא)?

phrases.english: If so, even regarding what he fixed [as the wage], too!
Why then is it taught:
A craftsman says: 'You fixed two [coins] for me,'

phrases.aramaic: וְהַלָּה אוֹמֵר ״לֹא קָצַצְתִּי לְךָ אֶלָּא אַחַת״ –
phrases.english: and the other says: 'I fixed only one for you' —
the one who takes from his fellow bears the burden of proof?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the earlier reason (טרוד בפועליו) for the worker's oath.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reason that the employer is busy with his workers and forgets.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the employer's memory is unreliable, the worker should be able to swear about the agreed amount too. Yet the ברייתא requires proof.

steps.title: The agreed wage is something he surely remembers
steps.stepSummary: An employer is busy and may forget whether he paid, but he definitely remembers what wage he agreed to.
steps.simpleTranslation: The agreed wage — he certainly remembers it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that being busy only affects remembering whether he paid. It does not affect remembering the deal he made.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'busy' reason is limited to the act of payment, which happens over and over with many workers. The agreed wage is a single deliberate deal, so the employer remembers it. That is why a dispute over the amount follows the normal rule of proof.

phrases.english: The fixing [of the wage] — he certainly remembers it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: the busy-employer reason applies to payment, not to the agreement.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Being busy makes the employer unreliable about everything to do with wages.
steps.terutzMaskana: He forgets only whether he paid. He surely remembers the agreed amount.

steps.title: Then the worker should also swear after the deadline
steps.stepSummary: If the employer may forget whether he paid, that should be true after the deadline too. Yet a ברייתא says that after the deadline the worker cannot swear and collect.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, even after his deadline passed he should swear and collect! Why does a ברייתא teach: if the deadline passed and the employer did not pay him, the worker does not swear and collect?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the 'busy employer' reason again. Forgetting whether you paid should not depend on whether the deadline has passed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the agreed amount, here the dispute really is about payment, which is exactly what the employer might forget. So the busy-employer reason should apply even after the deadline. Yet the ברייתא limits the oath to within the deadline (בזמנו).

phrases.aramaic: אִי הָכִי, אֲפִילּוּ עָבַר זְמַנּוֹ נָמֵי!
phrases.english: If so, even when his time has passed, too!
Why then is it taught:
If his time passed and he did not give him [his wage] —
this one does not swear and collect?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אֲפִילּוּ עָבַר זְמַנּוֹ נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to the same reason, from a different ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reason that the employer is busy and forgets whether he paid.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Forgetting about payment does not depend on the deadline. So the oath should be allowed even after the deadline, yet the ברייתא forbids it.

steps.title: Presumption that the employer does not violate בל תלין
steps.stepSummary: After the deadline we presume the employer already paid, because he would not transgress the prohibition against delaying wages.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a presumption that an employer does not violate 'do not keep [wages] overnight'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that after the deadline a new factor appears: a חזקה that the employer obeyed the תורה and paid on time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before the deadline there is no such presumption, so the worker's oath is enough. Once the deadline has passed, the employer is presumed to have paid, since otherwise he would have violated בל תלין. That presumption outweighs the worker's oath.

keyTerms.meaning: The prohibition against holding back a worker's wages past the deadline (ויקרא 19:13)

phrases.aramaic: חֲזָקָה אֵין בַּעַל הַבַּיִת עוֹבֵר בְּ״בַל תָּלִין״.
phrases.english: There is a presumption that an employer does not violate 'do not keep overnight.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A new presumption that only applies after the deadline.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The busy-employer reason should apply equally before and after the deadline.
steps.terutzMaskana: After the deadline, the presumption that he did not violate בל תלין means he paid.

steps.title: But you said the employer is busy and forgets
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the presumption: how can we assume he paid on time if we already said he is busy and forgets?
steps.simpleTranslation: But you said that the employer is busy with his workers!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out an apparent contradiction. Earlier it said the employer forgets, and now it says he surely paid on time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A presumption that he obeyed בל תלין only works if he remembers to pay. But the whole basis for the worker's oath was that the employer forgets. The two claims seem to clash.

phrases.english: But didn't you say:
The employer is busy with his workers!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 4 using the original reason.
steps.kashyaTarget: The presumption that the employer does not violate בל תלין.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If he is busy and forgets, he might forget to pay even by the deadline, so the presumption fails.

steps.title: At the deadline, he makes a point of remembering
steps.stepSummary: Being busy only applies before the deadline. When the deadline arrives, the employer takes the obligation to heart and remembers.
steps.simpleTranslation: That applies only before the time of obligation arrives. When the time of obligation arrives, he takes it upon himself and remembers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by dividing the time. Before the deadline he may forget, but at the deadline he focuses and remembers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before the deadline there is no urgency, so a busy employer may lose track. When the prohibition of בל תלין is about to apply, he concentrates and makes sure to pay. So both statements are true, each at its own time.

keyTerms.meaning: He puts it on himself (takes it to heart)

phrases.english: These words —
apply before the time of obligation arrives;
when the time of obligation arrives —
he takes it upon himself and remembers.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction by time: before the deadline versus at the deadline.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The employer is busy and forgetful at all times.
steps.terutzMaskana: He forgets only before the deadline. At the deadline he takes care to remember and pay.

steps.title: Does the worker violate the ban on stealing?
steps.stepSummary: The worker also has a presumption on his side: he would not steal by demanding pay twice. So why should the employer's presumption win?
steps.simpleTranslation: And does a hired worker violate 'do not rob'?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the presumption answer from the other side. The worker also has a חזקה that he would not sin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we trust the employer not to violate בל תלין, we should equally trust the worker not to violate בל תגזול by claiming wages twice. The two presumptions seem to cancel out. So why does the employer win after the deadline?

keyTerms.meaning: And is it so that...? (a sharp rhetorical question)

phrases.english: And does a hired worker violate 'do not rob'?!
phrases.notes: He means: would the worker really demand pay he already got? ויקרא 19:13

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי שָׂכִיר עוֹבֵר מִשּׁוּם בַּל תִּגְזוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the presumption of step 4 by pointing to an equal presumption for the worker.
steps.kashyaTarget: Relying on the employer's presumption against violating בל תלין.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The worker equally has a presumption that he would not rob. So the employer's presumption should not decide the case.

steps.title: The employer has two presumptions
steps.stepSummary: The employer has two presumptions on his side: he would not violate בל תלין, and a worker does not wait to ask for his pay. Two outweigh the worker's one.
steps.simpleTranslation: With the employer there are two presumptions: one, that an employer does not violate 'do not keep overnight,' and one, that a worker does not delay his wages.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the employer's side is stronger. It has two presumptions against the worker's single one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Besides the presumption that the employer obeys the law, workers normally ask for their pay right away. So a worker who comes after the deadline was probably already paid. With two presumptions on his side, the employer is believed, and the worker cannot simply swear and collect.

keyTerms.meaning: With regard to, on the side of

steps.whatToRemember: A שכיר swears and collects only within the deadline. The employer surely remembers the agreed amount, and after the deadline he has two חזקות: he does not violate בל תלין, and a worker does not delay asking for his pay.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why the תקנה of the worker's oath is limited to בזמנו, and why a dispute over the amount follows the normal rule of proof.

phrases.aramaic: גַּבֵּי בַּעַל הַבַּיִת אִיכָּא תְּרֵי חֲזָקֵי:
phrases.english: With the employer there are two presumptions:

phrases.aramaic: חֲדָא דְּאֵין בַּעַל הַבַּיִת עוֹבֵר בְּ״בַל תָּלִין״,
phrases.english: one, that an employer does not violate 'do not keep overnight,'
and one, that a hired worker does not delay [asking for] his wages.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The employer's and worker's presumptions are equal and cancel out.
steps.terutzMaskana: The employer has two presumptions against the worker's one, so after the deadline the worker cannot swear and collect.

steps.title: The worker's oath only applies when he was hired in front of witnesses
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן in the name of שמואל limits the משנה: the worker swears and collects only when the hiring was witnessed. Without witnesses, the employer is believed when he says he paid, because he could have denied hiring him at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said in the name of שמואל: The משנה only taught this rule when the employer hired the worker in front of witnesses. But if he hired him without witnesses, the employer could have said, 'I never hired you.' So he can also say, 'I hired you, and I already paid you,' and he is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: A new statement limits when the משנה's rule (the worker swears and collects) applies. It only works if there were witnesses to the hiring.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If nobody saw the hiring, the employer could simply have said 'I never hired you,' and the worker would have no case. Since he chose the weaker claim, 'I hired you and paid,' we believe him. This reasoning, 'he could have said something better,' is called a מגו.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this when; it limits a ruling to a specific case
Since he could have said; the wording of a מגו argument
The rule that a person is believed in a claim because he could have made a stronger one

steps.confusionAlert: This does not cancel the משנה. The worker's right to swear and collect stays in place. It just only applies when the hiring itself is proven by witnesses.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a classic use of מגו, and the rest of this section of the גמרא tests whether this kind of מגו really works.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said in the name of Shmuel:
They only taught this where he hired him in front of witnesses,
phrases.notes: 'This' is the משנה's rule that the worker swears and collects his pay.

phrases.english: but if he hired him without witnesses,
since he could have said to him:
'I never hired you,'
he can also say to him:
'I hired you, and I gave you your wages.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from explaining why the worker swears to setting a limit on when that rule applies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The worker swears and collects only when the hiring was witnessed. Without witnesses, the employer is believed through a מגו.

steps.title: רבי יצחק confirms the ruling in the name of רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק tells רב נחמן that he is right, and that רבי יוחנן said the same thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק said to him: That is correct, and רבי יוחנן said the same.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק backs up רב נחמן's ruling by reporting that רבי יוחנן held the same view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the ruling has support from both a בבלי authority (שמואל) and an ארץ ישראל authority (רבי יוחנן). This makes it stronger.

keyTerms.meaning: And so said; brings another authority who agrees

phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak said to him: Well said,
and so said Rabbi Yochanan.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the ruling of step 9 with another authority.
steps.raayaObject: The ruling that the worker's oath only applies with witnesses to the hiring.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The same ruling reported in the name of רבי יוחנן.

steps.title: Did ריש לקיש disagree?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether naming only רבי יוחנן implies that ריש לקיש, his usual partner in debate, disagreed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean that ריש לקיש disagrees with him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a side question about the report in step 10: since only רבי יוחנן is named, did ריש לקיש hold differently?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש usually learned together and often argued. Naming only one of them might suggest the other did not agree.

keyTerms.meaning: From this it follows; an inference

phrases.english: Does it follow that Reish Lakish disagrees with him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what follows from the wording of רבי יצחק's report.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether ריש לקיש disagreed with רבי יוחנן's ruling.

steps.title: ריש לקיש was silent, either drinking or waiting
steps.stepSummary: Two versions explain why ריש לקיש said nothing: he was drinking, or he was waiting for רבי יוחנן to finish. Either way, his silence does not prove he disagreed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say he was drinking and so he was silent. Others say he was waiting for him to finish and so he was silent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that ריש לקיש simply did not speak at that moment, and gives two possible reasons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His silence had a practical cause, so we cannot learn from it that he agreed or that he disagreed. The question is left open.

phrases.english: Some say

phrases.aramaic: מִישְׁתָּא הֲוָה שָׁתֵי לֵיהּ וְשָׁתֵיק לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: he was drinking, and so he was silent,
and some say

phrases.aramaic: מִישְׁהָא הֲוָה שָׁהֵי לֵיהּ וּשְׁתֵיק לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: he was waiting for him to finish, and so he was silent.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי מִישְׁתָּא הֲוָה שָׁתֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 11.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ריש לקיש's silence came from drinking or waiting, so it proves nothing about his view.

steps.title: רב also taught the same ruling
steps.stepSummary: A second report: רב מנשיא בר זביד in the name of רב gives the same limit, with the same מגו reasoning.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also said: רב מנשיא בר זביד said in the name of רב: The משנה only taught this rule when the worker was hired in front of witnesses. But if he was hired without witnesses, since the employer could have said 'I never hired you,' he can also say 'I hired you, and I paid you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another tradition, from רב, that says exactly the same thing as שמואל in step 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing new is added to the law. Its purpose is to show that both רב and שמואל held this ruling, which makes it very strong.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also stated; brings another tradition that agrees

phrases.english: It was also stated:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב מְנַשְּׁיָא בַּר זְבִיד, אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rav Menashya bar Zevid said in the name of Rav:
They only taught this where he hired him in front of witnesses,
but if he hired him without witnesses,
since he could have said to him:
'I never hired you,'
he can also say to him:
'I hired you, and I gave you your wages.'

steps.whatToRemember: Both רב and שמואל (and also רבי יוחנן) agree: without witnesses to the hiring, the employer is believed through a מגו.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 9 with a matching tradition from רב.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The same ruling in the name of רב, reported by רב מנשיא בר זביד.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא praises the ruling
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא says this ruling is excellent.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא said: How excellent this teaching is!
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר חמא praises the מגו ruling. This sets up the next step, where רבא will question it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The praise is not a new law. It opens a short debate about whether this kind of מגו reasoning really holds up.

phrases.english: Rami bar Chama said:
How excellent is this teaching!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Praises the ruling of steps 9 and 13, setting up רבא's challenge.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Praise for the מגו ruling, with no new law.

steps.title: רבא: by this logic the bailee's oath could never happen
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges the ruling. If a person is believed because he could have denied everything, then a שומר who says the item was lost by accident should be believed without an oath. But the Torah requires a שבועת שומרין!
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: What is so excellent about it? If so, how can you ever find the oath of a שומר that the Torah requires? Since the שומר could have said, 'This never happened,' he can also say, 'The item was lost by accident,' and be believed without an oath!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks the מגו ruling by showing that, if it were true, it would cancel a Torah law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah says a שומר who claims the item was lost by accident must swear. But usually he could have denied ever receiving it. With a מגו like this, he would be believed and never need to swear. So the Torah's oath would never apply, which cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: The oath the Torah requires of a person watching someone else's item
How can you find it; when would this ever happen
They were lost by accident, beyond the watcher's control
These things never happened; a total denial

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying a שומר is never believed. He is saying that if this מגו logic were correct, the Torah's oath would have no case left to apply to.

phrases.english: Rava said to him: What is its excellence?
If so, the oath of bailees
that the Merciful One required,
how can you ever find it?
Since he could say to him
'These things never happened,'
he can say to him, 'They were lost by accident'!
phrases.notes: So he should be believed without any oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי מְעַלְּיוּתָא? אִם כֵּן, שְׁבוּעַת שׁוֹמְרִין דְּחַיֵּיב רַחֲמָנָא הֵיכִי מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רמי בר חמא's praise by challenging the ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: The מגו reasoning of רב and שמואל (steps 9 and 13).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If 'he could have denied everything' frees a person from an oath, then a שומר claiming accident would never swear, which cancels the Torah's שבועת שומרין.

steps.title: The oath applies when the item was deposited with witnesses
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא answers רבא: the Torah's oath fits a case where the owner deposited the item in front of עדים, so the שומר cannot deny the deposit ever happened.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is where the owner deposited the item with him in front of witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר חמא defends his ruling. He shows a case where the שומר has no מגו of 'it never happened,' so the Torah's oath still has a job.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's challenge assumed the שומר could always say 'you never gave me anything.' If עדים saw the deposit, that denial is useless. So there is no מגו, and the שומר who claims an accident must swear.

keyTerms.meaning: He deposited (gave an item to be watched)
Since he could have made a stronger claim, he is believed on his weaker claim

phrases.english: Where he deposited it with him in front of witnesses.
phrases.notes: This is רמי בר חמא answering רבא's question from the last step.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's קשיא by narrowing the case of שבועת שומרין
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The שבועת שומרין seems useless, since the שומר always has a מגו
steps.terutzMaskana: When עדים saw the deposit, there is no מגו of denial, so the oath is needed

steps.title: He could still say he returned it
steps.stepSummary: רבא objects: even with עדים, the שומר could say 'I already gave it back,' so he still has a מגו for claiming an accident.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since he could say to him, 'I returned it to you,' he should be believed when he says, 'It was lost by accident!'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks the answer. The עדים block the claim 'it never happened,' but they do not block the claim 'I gave it back.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Returning a deposit does not need witnesses, so 'I returned it' would be believed. That gives the שומר a new מגו for 'it was lost by accident.' So the oath would again have no use.

keyTerms.meaning: Since he could say (the wording of a מגו)
They were lost by accident (אונס, beyond his control)

phrases.english: Since he can say to him,
"I returned it to you,"
he can say to him, "They were lost by accident"!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִתּוֹךְ שֶׁיָּכוֹל לוֹמַר לוֹ הֶחְזַרְתִּיו לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the case of עדים by finding a different מגו
steps.kashyaTarget: רמי בר חמא's answer that a deposit with עדים removes the מגו
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A claim of 'I returned it' is still believable, so the מגו stays and the oath is still useless

steps.title: The oath applies when the item was deposited with a document
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא answers again: the case is one where the deposit was recorded in a שטר, so the שומר cannot believably say he returned it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is where he deposited it with him with a document.
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר חמא gives a stronger case. Here the שומר has neither the claim 'it never happened' nor the claim 'I gave it back.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner still holds the שטר, that shows the item was not returned. A שומר who really returned it would have taken back the שטר. So 'I returned it' is not believed, there is no מגו, and the oath is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: A document (here, a written receipt for the deposit)

phrases.english: Where he deposited it with him with a document.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's second objection by narrowing the case further
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Even with עדים, the שומר can say 'I returned it'
steps.terutzMaskana: With a שטר, 'I returned it' is not believed, so there is no מגו and the oath applies
steps.whatToRemember: The ruling of רב and שמואל that רמי בר חמא praised stands: the Torah's שבועת שומרין is for a case where the שומר has no מגו, such as when the deposit was made with a שטר.

steps.title: Both agree on how a deposit must be returned
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא learns from this exchange that רבא and רמי בר חמא both hold: a deposit made with עדים need not be returned with עדים, but a deposit made with a שטר must be returned with עדים.
steps.simpleTranslation: We can learn that both of them hold: one who deposits with his friend in front of witnesses does not need to be given it back in front of witnesses. With a document, it must be given back in front of witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא steps back and draws a general rule from the back-and-forth between רבא and רמי בר חמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said 'I returned it' works even when there were עדים, so returning does not need עדים. רמי בר חמא did not argue with that point. Instead he moved to a שטר, showing that both agree a שטר changes things and requires עדים for the return.

keyTerms.meaning: By inference, we can learn from this

phrases.english: This implies that both of them hold:
phrases.notes: "Both" means רבא and רמי בר חמא.

phrases.english: One who deposits with his friend in front of witnesses —
he does not need to return it to him in front of witnesses;
with a document — he needs to return it to him in front of witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a general rule from the exchange in steps 16 to 18
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A deposit made with עדים may be returned without עדים. A deposit made with a שטר must be returned in front of עדים.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a practical rule in monetary law: how the deposit was made decides what proof of return is needed.
steps.whatToRemember: עדים at the deposit do not require עדים at the return. A שטר at the deposit does require עדים at the return.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא praises רב ששת with a verse
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא applies the פסוק about דוד taking words to heart to רב ששת, who took teachings seriously and searched for sources about them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא would read this verse about רב ששת: "And דוד laid up these words in his heart."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new point. This line praises רב ששת and sets up a story that shows why he earned that praise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse describes someone who keeps words in his heart and thinks them through. רב ששת did the same with the rulings in this סוגיא by looking for ברייתות that support or challenge them. The next step gives the example.

keyTerms.meaning: He read (applied) a verse about him
And he laid it up in his heart

phrases.english: Rami bar Chama would read
about Rav Sheshet:
"And David laid up these words in his heart."

steps.triggerLanguage: קָרֵי רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא עֲלֵיהּ דְּרַב שֵׁשֶׁת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section that praises רב ששת and leads into his search for a source
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב ששת took teachings to heart and searched for sources about them

steps.title: רב ששת asks רבה בר שמואל about a hired worker
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת meets רבה בר שמואל and asks whether he knows any ברייתא about a שכיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: For רב ששת met רבה בר שמואל and said to him: Do you teach anything about a hired worker?
steps.whatsHappening: This is the story behind the praise. רב ששת goes looking for a source about a שכיר, the subject of the earlier ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the סוגיא gave a limit on when a שכיר swears and collects. רב ששת wants a ברייתא to check that ruling against, so he asks a scholar who knows ברייתות.

keyTerms.meaning: Does the master teach anything (any ברייתא)?

phrases.aramaic: דְּאַשְׁכְּחֵיהּ רַב שֵׁשֶׁת לְרַבָּה בַּר שְׁמוּאֵל,
phrases.english: For Rav Sheshet met Rabba bar Shmuel,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: תָּנֵי מָר מִידֵּי בְּשָׂכִיר?
phrases.english: he said to him: Does the master teach anything about a hired worker?
phrases.notes: "The master" is a polite way to say "you."

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאַשְׁכְּחֵיהּ רַב שֵׁשֶׁת לְרַבָּה בַּר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the example that explains the praise in step 20
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רבה בר שמואל knows a ברייתא about a שכיר

steps.title: The ברייתא: a worker within his time swears and collects
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר שמואל quotes a ברייתא. A שכיר who claims his wages within the payment period swears and collects. This applies when the worker says 'you didn't pay me' and the employer says 'I paid you.'
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Yes, I teach: A hired worker within his time swears and takes. How so? When he said, 'You hired me and did not give me my wages,' and the other says, 'I hired you and gave you your wages.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר שמואל answers yes and quotes the ברייתא. It describes the case where the worker swears and collects.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a claimant needs proof, but here חז"ל let the worker swear and collect. The ברייתא limits this to a dispute about whether he was paid at all. Both sides agree on the hiring, and they argue only about payment.

keyTerms.meaning: Within his time (the period when wages are due)
And the other one (here, the employer)

phrases.english: He said to him: Yes, we learned:
A hired worker within his time — swears and takes.
How so — when he said to him:
"You hired me and did not give me my wages,"
and the other says:
"I hired you and gave you your wages";

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב ששת's question by quoting a ברייתא
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A ברייתא: a שכיר within his time swears and collects when the dispute is only about whether he was paid

steps.title: An argument about the amount: the claimant must bring proof
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: if the worker says the agreed wage was two and the employer says it was one, the worker cannot swear and collect. Whoever wants to take money must bring proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he said to him, 'You set two for me,' and the other says, 'I set only one for you,' the one who takes from his friend must bring the proof.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends by showing where the special oath does not apply: a dispute about how much was promised.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worker's special oath covers only the question of whether he was paid. When they argue about the agreed amount, the normal rule returns: הַמּוֹצִיא מֵחֲבֵירוֹ עָלָיו הָרְאָיָה. The worker needs proof to collect the larger sum.

keyTerms.meaning: You set (agreed on) a fixed wage
One who wants to take money from another must bring proof

steps.confusionAlert: The worker does not lose his oath because he is less trusted. As the גמרא explained in step 2, the oath rests on the employer forgetting whether he paid, and an employer surely remembers the amount he agreed to.

phrases.english: But if he said to him: "You set two for me,"
phrases.notes: "Two" means two coins as his wage.

phrases.english: and the other says:
"I set only one for you" —
the one who takes from his friend, the proof is on him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל אָמַר לוֹ שְׁתַּיִם קָצַצְתָּ לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא by giving the case where the worker does not swear and collect
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: In a dispute about the amount of the wage, the worker needs proof and cannot swear and collect
steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא is the source רב ששת found. The גמרא will now use it in connection with the earlier ruling about a שכיר.

steps.title: Inference: the first clause needs no proof
steps.stepSummary: Since the סיפא of the ברייתא requires proof, רב ששת infers that the רישא works without proof. That contradicts רב and שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the last part of the ברייתא talks about needing proof, the first part must be a case with no proof.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת reads the two halves of the ברייתא against each other. He infers that in the first half the worker swears and collects even without any proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סיפא (the argument about whether the wage was two or one) ends with 'whoever wants to take money must bring proof.' Mentioning proof only there suggests the רישא ('you didn't pay me') needs no proof at all. רב and שמואל had said the worker swears and collects only if עדים saw him being hired, so this reading of the ברייתא challenges them.

keyTerms.meaning: The first clause of a ברייתא or משנה
The last clause of a ברייתא or משנה
Proof, here meaning testimony of עדים
'Since...' A way of drawing an inference by contrasting two parts of a text

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא never says out loud that the רישא needs no proof. That is רב ששת's inference, drawn from the fact that proof is mentioned only in the סיפא.

phrases.english: Since the latter clause is with proof
phrases.notes: This points back to 'whoever wants to take money must bring proof' in the second half of the ברייתא.

phrases.english: the first clause is without proof.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא מִדְּסֵיפָא בִּרְאָיָה הָוֵי רֵישָׁא בְּלֹא רְאָיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from the ברייתא quoted in steps 22-23
steps.kashyaTarget: רב and שמואל's ruling that the שכיר swears and collects only when there are עדים that he was hired
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Proof is required only in the סיפא, so the רישא implies the worker swears and collects even without proof of being hired.

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק begins to respond
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק is introduced as the one who will answer the inference. His words follow in the next part of the גמרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said:
steps.whatsHappening: This line only introduces a speaker. The גמרא is setting up רב נחמן בר יצחק's response, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing has been answered yet. Based on the flow, we expect רב נחמן בר יצחק to explain the ברייתא so that רב ששת's inference does not have to follow.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces a response to the inference in step 24
steps.terutzResolutionType: Not yet stated. Only the speaker is introduced here.
